newsitem.title: ITALY: Ciampi wants Italian pension adjustment soon.
newsitem.headline: Ciampi wants Italian pension adjustment soon.

text.p: Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in an interview published on Monday that some adjustment to Italy's pensions spending was "probable" and as far as he was concerned, the soooner it happened the better.

"At the moment we don't have definitive data on how the 1995 reform has gone," Ciampi said in an interview with La Stampa, referring to a landmark 1995 pensions reform deal that is due to be reviewed next year.
"However, it is probable that some adjustment will be necessary to guarantee more stringent control of spending and to keep our social protection system efficient.
"My thesis is that the sooner we carry out this adjustment, the better," Ciampi said.

Italy's generous pensions system is a highly politically sensitive issue. The hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which lends vital support to Prime Minister Romano Prodi in parliament, has vowed to bring down the government if social spending is cut.

Welfare state reform also has become a more pressing issue as Italy tries to bring its state finances into line in order to meet the economic criteria that will allow it to be among the founding members of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Ciampi said the matter of welfare reform had been touched upon at a weekend meeting in Berlin of finance ministers from the G7 industrlialised nations. But Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the subject was discussed only in general terms and quickly moved to smoothe potentially ruffled feathers.
"Pensions, social security and reform of the social state will be done in Rome, not Berlin," he promised.
The leader of Italy's biggest party stepped into the debate on Monday, calling for a full debate to be held with union leaders on the whole welfare state.

Massimo D'Alema, leader of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left, suggested in an interview with Il Messaggero newspaper "proposing to the unions to hold a debate not only on pensions but on the whole social state".
He added: "Maybe they would accept that."
Unions, backed by Communist Refoundation, have fiercely opposed moves to bring forward discussions of the 1995 pensions deal which were originally scheduled to begin in 1998.
Armando Cossutta, a senior figure in the Communist Refoundation, warned on Sunday that "if it touches pensions and health, this government is dead".
D'Alema said Communist Refoundation was wrong to try to impose "diktats day in day out".
"We are facing a very complex question -- reform of the welfare state," he said. "We must face it with open dialogue between all political forces with no vetoes or blackmail."
